drills.q: Rank stored, reflected, and DOM-based XSS by real-world severity and explain why.
drills.a: Stored (highest -- persists server-side, hits every viewer with no extra attacker action) > reflected (needs a victim to click a specific crafted link) > DOM-based (client-only, never touches the server, increasingly common in SPA-heavy codebases and often missed by server-side scanning).

drills.q: Does httpOnly on a session cookie stop XSS? Be precise.
drills.a: No -- it stops exfiltration of the raw cookie value via JS, but a live XSS payload can still make authenticated requests as the victim while executing, since the browser still attaches the httpOnly cookie automatically. It bounds blast radius, doesn't prevent the incident.

drills.q: Explain how CSP defends against XSS even when an attacker successfully injects a script tag.
drills.a: A strict CSP (script-src 'self' 'nonce-X') makes the browser refuse to execute any script lacking the correct per-response nonce. The attacker's injected tag can't know that nonce, so even though present in the DOM, the browser won't execute it -- CSP prevents execution, not injection.

drills.q: A junior engineer claims 'we don't need CSRF tokens, our API only accepts application/json.' Evaluate.
drills.a: Provides SOME protection since basic HTML forms can't natively set arbitrary Content-Type, but an attacker's page can use fetch()/XHR with a custom Content-Type for a cross-origin request -- whether it succeeds depends on CORS, which blocks response-reading not request-sending, so the request still executes server-side. Real but incomplete; SameSite + explicit token remain load-bearing.

drills.q: What does CORS actually protect against, and what's the most common misunderstanding?
drills.a: CORS is a browser-enforced relaxation of same-origin policy letting a server opt specific origins into having their JS read a cross-origin response. It protects the browser's user from a malicious page reading data from a site the user is authenticated to -- it does NOT stop a direct non-browser request (curl, server-to-server) from reaching the server at all. Common mistake: treating it as a server-hardening/auth control.

drills.q: If CORS doesn't stop requests, why does a misconfigured CORS policy matter at all?
drills.a: The dangerous combination is reflecting the request's Origin header back unconditionally AND setting Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true -- this lets a malicious page make an authenticated cross-origin request via the victim's own browser and successfully READ the response containing private data, a real confidentiality breach even though the request was never blocked.

drills.q: Walk through the exact attack chain of the 2019 Capital One breach.
drills.a: A misconfigured WAF on EC2 had an SSRF vulnerability; the attacker made it fetch http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role>, the unauthenticated-by-design metadata endpoint, retrieving temporary IAM credentials. Those credentials had S3 read access, and the attacker exfiltrated 100M+ customer records. Chain: SSRF -> metadata credential theft -> S3 exfiltration, one crafted request.

drills.q: Would IMDSv2 alone have prevented the Capital One-style breach, and what would it NOT have fixed?
drills.a: Likely yes for this specific pattern -- IMDSv2 requires a session-token handshake (PUT for a token, then GET with it) that a basic SSRF-controlled single GET can't easily replicate. But it's a mitigation for THIS vector only; the same underlying WAF SSRF bug could still reach other internal, non-metadata infrastructure.

drills.q: Why is blocklisting SSRF targets fragile compared to allowlisting?
drills.a: Blocklists must anticipate decimal/octal IP encodings, redirect chains that pass initial validation then redirect to a blocked address, and DNS rebinding (hostname resolves safely at check-time, maliciously at request-time, since DNS resolution and the HTTP request are separate steps). An allowlist of exact permitted hosts sidesteps all of this.

drills.q: A team disables CSRF protection on an internal admin API because 'it's only called by our own frontend.' What's the flaw?
drills.a: If the API is cookie-authenticated and reachable from a browser, it's fully CSRF-vulnerable regardless of intended caller -- an unrelated external page can trick the admin's browser into firing a request using the admin's valid session cookie. 'Only called by our frontend' describes intended usage, not enforced usage. Network segmentation doesn't help either, since the victim's own browser (which has network access) is the one making the request.

drills.q: Design mitigation for a 'fetch and preview this URL' feature that must accept arbitrary user-supplied URLs by nature -- where pure allowlisting of hosts isn't possible.
drills.a: Route the fetch through a dedicated, network-isolated proxy service with no route to internal infrastructure, cloud metadata, or private IP ranges, containing blast radius architecturally. Layer on: resolve and validate the IP (not just hostname) immediately before firing the request to narrow the DNS-rebinding window, strict timeout/size limits, and never auto-follow redirects without re-validating the target.

drills.q: Your CSP has been in Report-Only mode for six months with zero violations. Should you flip to enforcing, and what could go wrong?
drills.a: Zero reports is promising but insufficient alone -- Report-Only only surfaces violations from traffic that actually occurred, missing rarely-hit routes or seasonal features. Cross-check against a full route/code-path crawl before flipping, consider staged rollout, and keep violation reporting active even after enforcing, since CSP failures fail silently client-side with no server-visible error.
